the glycosphingoglycolipids with negatively-charged terminal groups are able to inhibit the binding of mucosal strains of P. aeruginoga to rabbit bladder mucosal cells.
P. aeruginosis adhesion to the bladder mucosa is a multistep process involving the interaction between bacterial adhesins and the membrane glycosphigolipids of rabbit bladder epithelial cells.

the interaction between the adhesins of P. aeruginoga and the receptors of bladder mucosal cell membranes is a multistep process in which the first contact is made by the bacterial fimbrial subunits and the second by the carbohydrate moieties of glycolipids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
P. aeruginosaspecific adhesin binds to glycolipids containing galactose, sialic acid, and/or sulfate residues.

P. aeruginosis adhesion to the bladder mucosal cells involves glycolipids as receptor and that these glycolipids have a negative charge in their terminal groups, probably because of the presence of sialic acid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the glycosphingoglycolipids are the most important bacterial receptors on the bladder mucosal cell membrane.

Pseudomonas adhesion to rabbit bladder mucosal cells is a receptor-mediated process, and the glycosphingoglycolipids with negatively charges terminal groups seem to play an important role in this interaction.
